sections.name: Top stories
sections.label: Top stories
sections.glance: Claude Fable 5.2 on top of every independent board, Anthropic's IPO terms and its short-term compute bill, NVIDIA's founder out as chief executive, three ways AI keys leaked, and an outside verdict on a machine-checked physics proof.
sections.lead: Five stories. One is a model and one is the economics behind models: the new leader's price fell while its cost per task rose, and the lab that made it told investors its demand outran the compute it had contracted. One is the industry's largest supplier losing its chief executive in a month of credit stress and local votes against data centres. One is security: the keys that pay for AI leaked through traces, CI and a settings file. The last is what happens when machine-checked mathematics meets human reviewers.

sections.name: Models & releases
sections.label: Models
sections.glance: Gemini 4 Carbon opened to developers and Hydrogen replaced Flash, Kimi K3.1 Pro's weights arrived, Qwen4-Max and Muse Ember launched closed, Inkling 2 Small opened its weights, three Chinese MoE designs, and two measuring tools fixed. Holds the index chart.
sections.lead: The fortnight's releases sorted themselves by price. At the top, Google opened its strongest model to developers; in the middle, Hydrogen, Qwen4-Max and Muse Ember compete on cost per task rather than per token. The open-weight models got bigger and more varied in architecture, yet on Artificial Analysis's board the distance from the best open model to the best closed one grew. Two items are about the instruments: a benchmark that hardened its own graders and an index that measured how much accuracy hosting providers lose.

sections.name: Research & papers
sections.label: Research
sections.glance: Dense rewards against GRPO at matched tokens (new paper page), GRPO with group-dependent rewards, monitors evaded by reward hackers, three precision papers, two sparse and linear attention papers, and agent evaluation errors. Holds the token-budget animation.
sections.lead: Most of the fortnight's research asked one question of a familiar method: compared on what? A process reward wins per update and loses per token; FP4 matches BF16 on loss and lags on rare facts; a quantised model looks worse until restarts and batch sizes are given the same scrutiny; one agent beat another because half its episodes were never graded. Read each result with the denominator its authors chose.

sections.name: Industry
sections.label: Industry
sections.glance: OpenAI's round, two acquisitions of coding-agent tooling, Cerebras' quarter, China's draft export controls on model weights, and a bank restricting a coding agent.
sections.lead: Beyond the top stories, the money moved toward tools for coding agents (OpenAI buying Pierre, Meta buying Conductor) and toward the companies that host models; policy reached the weights themselves, with China's draft counting a model run abroad as an export.

sections.name: Compute & chips
sections.label: Compute
sections.glance: Two more TPU 8 systems, AMD's first MI450 revenue, Marvell buying Lumentum for optics, weights that reveal which GPU initialised them, and gas, sites and 800V DC for power.
sections.lead: New silicon reached customers (AMD's MI450 racks) or was announced as variants (two TPU 8 systems), while the deals and the forensics were about what sits around the chips: the optical links between them, the power under them, and the traces their random number generators leave in published weights.

sections.name: Dev tooling & agents
sections.label: Dev tools
sections.glance: Code Mode in Claude Code, server-side message threads, how Anthropic builds agent memory, a 1,000-agent team, decision models from four vendors, the token cost of MCP against a CLI, serving engine releases and Git rebuilt for agents.
sections.lead: Two threads ran through the tools. One is cutting what a model has to read: code that calls tools instead of one call per turn, threads that keep the conversation on the server, decision heads that return a probability instead of text, and a measurement of what tool definitions and results cost. The other is infrastructure built for many agents at once: a shared database as a coordination bus, and Git servers rebuilt for agent push volume.

sections.name: Security
sections.label: Security
sections.glance: Eleven bypasses of Codex's approval monitor, an email in a User-Agent header, a fake Claude Code package, the CVE count from Anthropic's vulnerability search, an OpenSSH bypass on musl, and exposed app data.
sections.lead: Besides the leaked keys in Top stories, the fortnight's security items are about the layers meant to catch an agent: the monitor that approves its actions, the checks on what it sends out, and the packages and apps built around it.

sections.name: Talk of the town
sections.label: Talk of the town
sections.glance: Technical debt paid off by attackers, open-sourcing AI-written code, leaving a harness over prompt churn, a reasoning-summary scare, and what AI-written code does to codebases.
sections.lead: The long comment threads were about the cost of AI in software rather than its capability: bugs found faster than they can be fixed, harnesses that change under their users, and codebases that become harder to change.

dense: Are Dense Rewards Worth Their Tokens in GRPO? (paper page)

glance.label: At a glance
glance.lead: Two weeks, 2026-11-02 to 2026-11-16: 65 items across models, research, industry, chips, developer tools, security and the fortnight's arguments, each with its sources. The issue was written from the sources on 2026-11-16; where a claim rests on one outlet or a vendor, its card says so. This tab is the fortnight in one screen; every section has its own tab with the items in full.
glance.theme: The fortnight's theme: the denominators changed. The new top model is cheaper per token and the most expensive per task; a process reward wins per update and loses per token; an AI lab's quarter turned on the price of compute bought late rather than on demand; and an index of open against closed models moved because the closed end moved. The [[index chart|t-models|v-ix]] shows the fortnight's releases on one scale, and the [[token-budget animation|t-research|v-budget]] shows how a dense reward spends the same budget as GRPO on far fewer updates.
